screens.title: Comprehensive Smart Contract Testing with Hardhat and Waffle
screens.narratorSegment: Testing is the safety net that protects immutable smart contracts. In this chapter you will learn how Hardhat creates an isolated runtime for tests, how ethers. js enables contract deployment and interaction inside tests, and how Waffle extends assertions with matchers designed for Ethereum. We’ll work through concrete examples, starting with a simple Counter contract and then writing unit tests that verify normal behavior, event emission, and failure modes like reverts. Along the way you'll see how to use Mocha's describe/it structure and the beforeEach hook to keep tests deterministic and independent. You will also practice simulating multiple signers and using the connect method to test role-based interactions. The goal is not just to pass tests, but to think like an attacker or auditor: cover edge cases, validate error messages, and reason about state transitions. By the end you will be able to write clear tests that catch regressions before deployment and use Waffle matchers to assert events, reverts, and balance changes. Consider this lesson an essential step toward shipping secure contracts—what single edge case will you test first?

Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Overview
Comprehensive Smart Contract Testing
Use Hardhat, ethers.js, and Waffle matchers to write deterministic tests that catch logic errors and reverts.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson

Set up tests, use Mocha structure, deploy contracts with ethers, assert behaviors with Waffle, and avoid common pitfalls.

Why it matters

A failed test that simulates an attacker or bad input is cheaper than a production exploit. Tests are your first audit.

What you will practice
  • Writing deterministic unit tests for Counter and MyToken examples
  • Using beforeEach to reset state for each test
  • Asserting reverts, events, and balance changes with Waffle
Explore Key Topics
Deterministic Tests
Hardhat network isolates runs so each test starts fresh; use beforeEach for repeatability.
Waffle Matchers
Matchers make it easy to assert events, reverts, and balance changes precisely.
Multi-signer Tests
Simulate different accounts using getSigners and contract.connect for realistic interactions.
Visual Concept
Test Loop
Compile → Deploy (local) → Run tests → Reset state
Example flow
Counter contract: increment, expect value, decrement, expect revert when zero.
Key Outcome
Tests catch logic and edge cases so deployments are safer and more predictable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will reliably write and run unit tests for Solidity smart contracts using Hardhat, ethers. js, and Waffle. First, you will understand why testing matters for immutable contracts and how Hardhat's local network produces repeatable test runs. Second, you will be able to structure tests using Mocha's describe and it blocks and use beforeEach to reset state before each case. Third, you will use ethers. getContractFactory, deploy contracts, and call contract. connect to simulate different accounts. Fourth, you will apply Waffle matchers such as to. equal, to. be. revertedWith, and changeEtherBalance to assert precise behaviors, events, and balance changes. Each objective includes a short practice cue: set up a fresh test with beforeEach, deploy a Counter, assert increments and reverts, simulate two signers for transfers, and check emitted events. These skills matter because tests are your primary defense against bugs that cannot be trivially patched on-chain. As you practice, think in terms of both expected behavior and malicious or accidental edge cases. Which scenario will you test first?

Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Objectives — Part 2
Edge cases & events

You will explicitly test failure conditions such as require reverts and verify that important events are emitted so off-chain systems can respond reliably.

Activity
Write tests for MyToken: deployment supply, successful transfer, revert on insufficient balance, and Transfer event emission.
Running tests

Use npx hardhat test. Hardhat compiles, spins up a local network, deploys contracts, and runs test files inside test/ to produce deterministic failure traces.

Why this matters

Tests simulate user interactions and attacker cases before you ever deploy immutable code that could be costly to replace.

screens.title: Why testing is critical for smart contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contracts on a blockchain are fundamentally different from most server code because deployed bytecode is often immutable and public. This means a bug discovered after deployment can be impossible to fix without deploying a new contract and migrating users. Testing is therefore not optional; it is the first line of defense against costly mistakes. A good test suite does more than check happy paths: it verifies edge cases, input validation, access control, and explicit revert messages so front-end code and other contracts can react appropriately. For example, the Counter example included in this chapter shows both normal increments and a require-based revert when attempting to decrement at zero. That revert must be asserted in tests using Waffle's revertedWith matcher. A common misconception is that passing a few manual checks is enough; in practice, automated tests that run quickly and deterministically let you catch regressions during development and before deployment. To practice, aim to write tests that fail for the right reasons, then fix the contract. The desired outcome is a test suite that documents expected behaviors and prevents accidental changes from introducing vulnerabilities. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Why testing is critical
Definition

Testing here means automated unit tests that run on Hardhat's local network to exercise contract functions, state changes, events, and failure modes so deployments are safer.

Why it matters
  • Immutability makes post-deploy fixes costly and risky.
  • Automated tests document intended behavior for future maintainers.
  • Edge-case tests reproduce attacker-style inputs early.
Key Takeaway

Automated, isolated tests make immutable deployments predictable and auditable.

Concrete example
Counter contract: increment increases count, decrement requires count > 0. Tests should assert both the incremented value and that decrement reverts when count equals zero.
Common misconception
Mistake

Relying on manual testing or only happy-path tests misses failure modes; tests should include explicit revert assertions and role-based scenarios.

screens.title: How Hardhat runs tests
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat streamlines test execution by combining compilation, a local ephemeral network, and deployment of contracts for each test run. When you run npx hardhat test, Hardhat compiles contracts if necessary, launches the Hardhat Network, and executes Mocha test files from the test/ directory. Each test run starts with a clean state so tests remain deterministic. Within tests, Hardhat provides the ethers object via the Hardhat Runtime Environment; this lets you obtain contract factories, call deploy, and interact with signers provided by the network. Use beforeEach to deploy fresh contract instances so related tests don't share state. The local network is fast and resets between runs, which encourages frequent test execution during development. One common misconception is that running tests against a local network guarantees production behavior; tests reduce risk but do not replace audits or specialized runtime checks. Instead, treat the Hardhat test environment as a rapid feedback loop for contract logic. Practically, structure suites around describe blocks for features and keep test cases focused and independent. Which part of this loop would you inspect first when a test intermittently fails?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Hardhat test flow
Test execution architecture
  1. npx hardhat test compiles contracts if needed.
  2. Hardhat Network is launched locally and deterministically.
  3. Tests deploy contracts using ethers.getContractFactory and contract.deploy.
  4. Each test run starts from a clean state; use beforeEach for per-test setup.
Pro tip

Keep deployments in beforeEach to ensure test isolation and avoid state leakage across cases.

Concrete example
When a test uses ethers.getSigners(), the Hardhat Network provides multiple signer objects so you can simulate different users without connecting to a real network.
Common misconception

Passing tests in Hardhat does not guarantee production safety; tests reduce risk but should be paired with audits and careful design.

screens.title: Counter contract and its tests
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine the Counter contract and the matching test file to see how behavior and assertions align. The Counter contract sets a public unsigned integer count, increments it, and decrements only when the count is greater than zero, otherwise it reverts with a clear message. The corresponding test file organizes tests with describe blocks: a top-level describe for the contract and nested describe sections for deployment, incrementation, and decrementation. A beforeEach hook obtains the ContractFactory, signers, deploys a fresh contract, and waits for deployment. Test cases use await when calling contract functions and Waffle's expect matcher to assert results. For example, after calling increment once, expect(await counter. getCount()). to. equal(1). For a revert test, use await expect(counter. decrement()). to. be. revertedWith("Count cannot go below zero"). This pattern—setup in beforeEach and clear, focused it cases—produces deterministic tests that document intended behavior. A common pitfall is forgetting await on a transaction, which can yield false positives or unresolved promises. When you write tests, ensure awaits are present and that state checks read the contract after transactions resolve. Try reading the provided Counter. sol and test/Counter. js snippets carefully to spot awaits and assertions.

keyIdea.text: Deploy fresh instances in beforeEach, await transactions, and assert both state and revert messages for thorough coverage.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Counter Walkthrough
Counter.sol (excerpt)
// contracts/Counter.sol // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT pragma solidity ^0.8.0; contract Counter { uint public count; constructor() { count = 0; } function increment() public { count++; } function decrement() public { require(count > 0, "Count cannot go below zero"); count--; } function getCount() public view returns (uint) { return count; } }
test/Counter.js (excerpt)
const { expect } = require("chai"); const { ethers } = require("hardhat"); describe("Counter", function () { let Counter; let counter; let owner; beforeEach(async function () { Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter"); [owner] = await ethers.getSigners(); counter = await Counter.deploy(); await counter.deployed(); }); it("Should set the initial count to 0", async function () { expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(0); }); it("Should increment the count by 1", async function () { await counter.increment(); expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(1); }); it("Should revert if count is already 0", async function () { await expect(counter.decrement()).to.be.revertedWith("Count cannot go below zero"); }); });
Common mistake

Missing await on transactions or not redeploying per test can cause flaky or interdependent tests.

screens.title: Waffle matchers you must know
screens.narratorSegment: Waffle extends Chai with matchers tailored to Ethereum testing. The most common matchers you will use are to. equal for strict value equality, to. be. revertedWith for asserting specific revert messages, and matchers for balance changes like to. changeEtherBalance. Use to. equal for checking returned view values or token balances after transactions. For failure cases that should revert, to. be. revertedWith confirms that a transaction fails with the expected message, which is essential for access control and input validation tests. For transfers and deposits, to. changeEtherBalance and related token balance matchers let you assert sender and recipient balance deltas while accounting for gas when appropriate. A typical mistake is asserting only an event was emitted without checking the emitted values; Waffle lets you assert event names and indexed arguments as well. When choosing a matcher, prefer the one that communicates intent clearly: equality for final state, revertedWith for failure reasons, and change matchers for precise economic effects. As you add these matchers into your suite, your tests will document both logic and economic behavior of contracts. Which matcher would you reach for first when testing a payment function?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Waffle Matchers
Common matchers
  • to.equal — Assert a returned value or a view reading equals the expected number or string.
  • to.be.revertedWith — Assert a transaction reverts with the specific error message.
  • to.changeEtherBalance — Assert that an account's Ether balance changed by an expected amount after a transaction.
Key Tip

Assert both the event and the state change when testing economic functions to avoid false confidence.

Concrete snippets
// Example assertions
expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(1);
await expect(counter.decrement()).to.be.revertedWith("Count cannot go below zero");
expect(await myToken.totalSupply()).to.equal(initialSupply);
await expect(() => depositBox.connect(addr1).deposit({ value: ethers.utils.parseEther("1") })).to.changeEtherBalance(addr1, ethers.utils.parseEther("-1"));
Misuse

Using to.equal on transactions that don't immediately return values can be misleading; read contract state after awaiting the transaction.

screens.title: Organizing tests with describe/it and beforeEach
screens.narratorSegment: Good test organization makes a suite easy to read and maintain. Mocha provides describe blocks to group related tests and it blocks for individual test cases. Use nested describe sections to separate feature areas, such as deployment, normal actions, and edge-case tests. The beforeEach hook runs prior to each it case inside its containing describe, making it the ideal place to deploy fresh contract instances and to obtain signers. This creates test isolation: when a test mutates state, the next test starts from a fresh contract, reducing flakiness. Keep each it block focused on a single assertion or closely related assertions; that way a failure pinpoints behavior precisely. Include small helper functions only when they improve clarity, and avoid long chains of setup inside an it block. A misconception is that fewer beforeEach calls improves speed; in practice, clarity and isolation outweigh a small per-test compile time. For example, in the Counter tests we deploy a new Counter in beforeEach and then assert either increment or a revert in separate it blocks. This pattern makes it obvious which case fails and why. When you write tests, ask whether each it block documents a single expectation users or integrators rely on.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Test Organization
Pattern: describe / it / beforeEach
Group
describe("Counter") groups tests related to the same contract or feature.
Case
it("Should increment") defines a single expectation and contains the actions and assertions for that case.
Setup
beforeEach(async () => { deploy fresh contract }) ensures isolation between it cases.
Check your understanding

If two it blocks depend on a shared mutated state, rewrite them to deploy a fresh instance per test to avoid coupling.

screens.title: Testing events and Transfer semantics
screens.narratorSegment: Events are the primary mechanism by which on-chain actions notify off-chain services and other contracts. Testing that the right events are emitted, with correct indexed arguments when appropriate, ensures that listeners such as front ends, analytics, or oracles can rely on those signals. The MyToken example included in this chapter emits Transfer on successful transfers. Tests should check both that Transfer is emitted and that its parameters match expectations, because a missing or malformed event breaks integrations downstream. A common mistake is asserting only state changes and not event emission. While state checks confirm the contract's internal status, event assertions validate the contract's external contract with off-chain systems. Use Waffle to assert events and their arguments reliably. For example, after a successful transfer, assert that Transfer was emitted with from, to, and value matching the transfer call. Also ensure that transfers that revert do not emit events. This combination of state and event assertions gives you stronger guarantees about how the contract behaves both internally and externally. Which listener in your stack would break if an event argument were incorrect?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Events & Transfer
Why test events

Events are consumed by wallets, front ends, and monitoring tools. If an event is missing or has wrong arguments, integrations will misbehave even when internal state looks correct.

Takeaway

Assert both state and event emission for critical actions like token transfers.

Concrete example (MyToken)
// After transfer
await expect(myToken.connect(owner).transfer(addr1.address, amount))
  .to.emit(myToken, 'Transfer')
  .withArgs(owner.address, addr1.address, amount);
Pitfall

Relying only on event presence without checking arguments hides subtle regressions in emitted data.

screens.title: Simulating multiple users with getSigners and connect
screens.narratorSegment: Testing with multiple signers is essential for contracts that allow different accounts to interact with the same state. Hardhat's ethers. getSigners returns a list of Signer objects representing funded accounts on the local network. Use these signers to simulate different roles: owner, caller, beneficiary, attacker. The contract. connect(signer) pattern creates a contract instance that sends transactions from the selected signer, which is how you test role-based constraints or permission checks. For example, to simulate addr1 calling decrement on the Counter, you call await counter. connect(addr1). decrement(); and then assert the expected state or reverts. A common pitfall is to read state using the default signer when the action was performed by another signer; always connect the signer that should perform the transaction. Additionally, when testing transfers or balance effects, use changeEtherBalance with the signer that initiated the transaction so gas costs are considered. Practically, structure tests with variables like owner, addr1, addr2 populated by await ethers. getSigners(), then reference them explicitly in tests. Which role in your contract would you assign to the second signer in your next test? Simulating multiple users with getSigners and connect means use getsigners and contract.connect(signer) to reproduce interactions from different accounts and validate access control and transfers.. In practical terms, test role-based behavior and cross-user interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Multi-signer Testing
Pattern
  1. Get signers: const [owner, addr1, addr2] = await ethers.getSigners();
  2. Deploy contract with one signer in beforeEach.
  3. Simulate actions: await contract.connect(addr1).someAction();
Reminder

Always connect the signer that should be the transaction sender; otherwise tests may not simulate real permission paths.

Concrete example
// Simulate addr1 decrementing after owner increment
await counter.increment();
await counter.connect(addr1).decrement();
expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(0);
Pitfall

Forgetting to contract.connect will perform the call from the default signer, giving a false impression of role access.

screens.title: Edge cases and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Many test failures stem from a small number of recurring pitfalls. First, missing await on transaction calls can leave promises unresolved and cause assertions to read stale state. Always await the transaction and any required confirmations before checking state. Second, tests that share mutated state produce interdependent failures; deploy fresh instances in beforeEach to avoid that. Third, failing to assert revert messages means a test might pass even when the wrong revert reason or side effects occur. Use to. be. revertedWith to lock the expected failure reason. Fourth, not testing multiple signers or edge cases like zero-values and overflows leaves potential attack paths untested. For example, failing to test a require branch such as decrement at zero would miss a critical error path. Finally, assuming 100% coverage equals security is a misconception — coverage helps find untested lines but does not guarantee correctness of logic or resilience against complex attack vectors. Address these pitfalls by writing small, focused tests for edge cases, using clear revert assertions, and simulating competitor or attacker behaviors where appropriate. Which pitfall have you seen in past tests?

screens.title: Running tests and reading Hardhat output
screens.narratorSegment: Running npx hardhat test compiles contracts and runs test files, producing console output that tells you which cases passed or failed and stack traces for failures. Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › MyToken Activity
Starter contract
// contracts/MyToken.sol // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT pragma solidity ^0.8.0; contract MyToken { string public name = "MyToken"; string public symbol = "MTK"; uint256 public totalSupply; mapping(address => uint256) public balances; constructor(uint256 initialSupply) { totalSupply = initialSupply; balances[msg.sender] = initialSupply; } function transfer(address recipient, uint256 amount) public returns (bool) { require(balances[msg.sender] >= amount, "Insufficient balance"); balances[msg.sender] -= amount; balances[recipient] += amount; emit Transfer(msg.sender, recipient, amount); return true; } function balanceOf(address account) public view returns (uint256) { return balances[account]; } event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value); }
Test starter
// test/MyToken.js const { expect } = require("chai"); const { ethers } = require("hardhat"); describe("MyToken", function () { let MyToken; let myToken; let owner; let addr1; let addr2; const initialSupply = ethers.utils.parseEther("1000"); // 1000 tokens beforeEach(async function () { MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyToken"); [owner, addr1, addr2] = await ethers.getSigners(); myToken = await MyToken.deploy(initialSupply); await myToken.deployed(); }); // Write your tests here! });
Activity steps
  1. Assert totalSupply equals initialSupply and owner balance equals initialSupply.
  2. Test successful transfer: balances change and Transfer event emits with correct args.
  3. Test transferring more than balance reverts with "Insufficient balance".
  4. Verify balanceOf returns correct balances after transfers.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Assessment Ideas
Access control assertion
Use to.be.revertedWith with the expected owner error message when testing calls from a non-owner signer. This confirms the contract enforces only-owner logic.
Example
await expect(pausable.connect(addr1).pause()).to.be.revertedWith("Ownable: caller is not the owner");
Balance change assertion
Use to.changeEtherBalance to assert a sender's Ether decreased by the expected amount after a deposit, and that the recipient increased, while accounting for gas.
Example
await expect(async () => await depositBox.connect(addr1).deposit({ value: ethers.utils.parseEther("1") })).to.changeEtherBalance(addr1, ethers.utils.parseEther("-1"));

fullNarratorScript:
Testing is the safety net that protects immutable smart contracts. In this chapter you will learn how Hardhat creates an isolated runtime for tests, how ethers. js enables contract deployment and interaction inside tests, and how Waffle extends assertions with matchers designed for Ethereum. We’ll work through concrete examples, starting with a simple Counter contract and then writing unit tests that verify normal behavior, event emission, and failure modes like reverts. Along the way you'll see how to use Mocha's describe/it structure and the beforeEach hook to keep tests deterministic and independent. You will also practice simulating multiple signers and using the connect method to test role-based interactions. The goal is not just to pass tests, but to think like an attacker or auditor: cover edge cases, validate error messages, and reason about state transitions. By the end you will be able to write clear tests that catch regressions before deployment and use Waffle matchers to assert events, reverts, and balance changes. Consider this lesson an essential step toward shipping secure contracts—what single edge case will you test first?

By the end of this chapter you will reliably write and run unit tests for Solidity smart contracts using Hardhat, ethers. js, and Waffle. First, you will understand why testing matters for immutable contracts and how Hardhat's local network produces repeatable test runs. Second, you will be able to structure tests using Mocha's describe and it blocks and use beforeEach to reset state before each case. Third, you will use ethers. getContractFactory, deploy contracts, and call contract. connect to simulate different accounts. Fourth, you will apply Waffle matchers such as to. equal, to. be. revertedWith, and changeEtherBalance to assert precise behaviors, events, and balance changes. Each objective includes a short practice cue: set up a fresh test with beforeEach, deploy a Counter, assert increments and reverts, simulate two signers for transfers, and check emitted events. These skills matter because tests are your primary defense against bugs that cannot be trivially patched on-chain. As you practice, think in terms of both expected behavior and malicious or accidental edge cases. Which scenario will you test first?

These objectives continue with practical testing habits and an activity you will complete. You will learn to test edge cases such as require() reverts, to test event emission so external listeners can depend on on-chain signals, and to simulate multiple roles interacting with a contract by connecting different signers. You will also adopt a habit of explicitly testing error messages when access control or input validation should block an action. The included hands-on activity asks you to write tests for a simple ERC-20-like MyToken contract: assert total supply, verify successful transfers emit an event, and verify transfers that exceed balance revert with the correct message. Finally, you'll practice running npx hardhat test and reading its output to diagnose failures. These skills help you audit state transitions and avoid regressions during refactors. As you practice, note that 100% line coverage is helpful but not a guarantee; use tests to reason about attack surfaces, then consider separate audits for critical contracts. Which failing test would most scare you if it ran in production?

Smart contracts on a blockchain are fundamentally different from most server code because deployed bytecode is often immutable and public. This means a bug discovered after deployment can be impossible to fix without deploying a new contract and migrating users. Testing is therefore not optional; it is the first line of defense against costly mistakes. A good test suite does more than check happy paths: it verifies edge cases, input validation, access control, and explicit revert messages so front-end code and other contracts can react appropriately. For example, the Counter example included in this chapter shows both normal increments and a require-based revert when attempting to decrement at zero. That revert must be asserted in tests using Waffle's revertedWith matcher. A common misconception is that passing a few manual checks is enough; in practice, automated tests that run quickly and deterministically let you catch regressions during development and before deployment. To practice, aim to write tests that fail for the right reasons, then fix the contract. The desired outcome is a test suite that documents expected behaviors and prevents accidental changes from introducing vulnerabilities. What one edge case would you add to an existing suite to increase confidence right away?

Hardhat streamlines test execution by combining compilation, a local ephemeral network, and deployment of contracts for each test run. When you run npx hardhat test, Hardhat compiles contracts if necessary, launches the Hardhat Network, and executes Mocha test files from the test/ directory. Each test run starts with a clean state so tests remain deterministic. Within tests, Hardhat provides the ethers object via the Hardhat Runtime Environment; this lets you obtain contract factories, call deploy, and interact with signers provided by the network. Use beforeEach to deploy fresh contract instances so related tests don't share state. The local network is fast and resets between runs, which encourages frequent test execution during development. One common misconception is that running tests against a local network guarantees production behavior; tests reduce risk but do not replace audits or specialized runtime checks. Instead, treat the Hardhat test environment as a rapid feedback loop for contract logic. Practically, structure suites around describe blocks for features and keep test cases focused and independent. Which part of this loop would you inspect first when a test intermittently fails?

Let's examine the Counter contract and the matching test file to see how behavior and assertions align. The Counter contract sets a public unsigned integer count, increments it, and decrements only when the count is greater than zero, otherwise it reverts with a clear message. The corresponding test file organizes tests with describe blocks: a top-level describe for the contract and nested describe sections for deployment, incrementation, and decrementation. A beforeEach hook obtains the ContractFactory, signers, deploys a fresh contract, and waits for deployment. Test cases use await when calling contract functions and Waffle's expect matcher to assert results. For example, after calling increment once, expect(await counter. getCount()). to. equal(1). For a revert test, use await expect(counter. decrement()). to. be. revertedWith("Count cannot go below zero"). This pattern—setup in beforeEach and clear, focused it cases—produces deterministic tests that document intended behavior. A common pitfall is forgetting await on a transaction, which can yield false positives or unresolved promises. When you write tests, ensure awaits are present and that state checks read the contract after transactions resolve. Try reading the provided Counter. sol and test/Counter. js snippets carefully to spot awaits and assertions.

Waffle extends Chai with matchers tailored to Ethereum testing. The most common matchers you will use are to. equal for strict value equality, to. be. revertedWith for asserting specific revert messages, and matchers for balance changes like to. changeEtherBalance. Use to. equal for checking returned view values or token balances after transactions. For failure cases that should revert, to. be. revertedWith confirms that a transaction fails with the expected message, which is essential for access control and input validation tests. For transfers and deposits, to. changeEtherBalance and related token balance matchers let you assert sender and recipient balance deltas while accounting for gas when appropriate. A typical mistake is asserting only an event was emitted without checking the emitted values; Waffle lets you assert event names and indexed arguments as well. When choosing a matcher, prefer the one that communicates intent clearly: equality for final state, revertedWith for failure reasons, and change matchers for precise economic effects. As you add these matchers into your suite, your tests will document both logic and economic behavior of contracts. Which matcher would you reach for first when testing a payment function?

Good test organization makes a suite easy to read and maintain. Mocha provides describe blocks to group related tests and it blocks for individual test cases. Use nested describe sections to separate feature areas, such as deployment, normal actions, and edge-case tests. The beforeEach hook runs prior to each it case inside its containing describe, making it the ideal place to deploy fresh contract instances and to obtain signers. This creates test isolation: when a test mutates state, the next test starts from a fresh contract, reducing flakiness. Keep each it block focused on a single assertion or closely related assertions; that way a failure pinpoints behavior precisely. Include small helper functions only when they improve clarity, and avoid long chains of setup inside an it block. A misconception is that fewer beforeEach calls improves speed; in practice, clarity and isolation outweigh a small per-test compile time. For example, in the Counter tests we deploy a new Counter in beforeEach and then assert either increment or a revert in separate it blocks. This pattern makes it obvious which case fails and why. When you write tests, ask whether each it block documents a single expectation users or integrators rely on.

Events are the primary mechanism by which on-chain actions notify off-chain services and other contracts. Testing that the right events are emitted, with correct indexed arguments when appropriate, ensures that listeners such as front ends, analytics, or oracles can rely on those signals. The MyToken example included in this chapter emits Transfer on successful transfers. Tests should check both that Transfer is emitted and that its parameters match expectations, because a missing or malformed event breaks integrations downstream. A common mistake is asserting only state changes and not event emission. While state checks confirm the contract's internal status, event assertions validate the contract's external contract with off-chain systems. Use Waffle to assert events and their arguments reliably. For example, after a successful transfer, assert that Transfer was emitted with from, to, and value matching the transfer call. Also ensure that transfers that revert do not emit events. This combination of state and event assertions gives you stronger guarantees about how the contract behaves both internally and externally. Which listener in your stack would break if an event argument were incorrect?

Testing with multiple signers is essential for contracts that allow different accounts to interact with the same state. Hardhat's ethers. getSigners returns a list of Signer objects representing funded accounts on the local network. Use these signers to simulate different roles: owner, caller, beneficiary, attacker. The contract. connect(signer) pattern creates a contract instance that sends transactions from the selected signer, which is how you test role-based constraints or permission checks. For example, to simulate addr1 calling decrement on the Counter, you call await counter. connect(addr1). decrement(); and then assert the expected state or reverts. A common pitfall is to read state using the default signer when the action was performed by another signer; always connect the signer that should perform the transaction. Additionally, when testing transfers or balance effects, use changeEtherBalance with the signer that initiated the transaction so gas costs are considered. Practically, structure tests with variables like owner, addr1, addr2 populated by await ethers. getSigners(), then reference them explicitly in tests. Which role in your contract would you assign to the second signer in your next test? Simulating multiple users with getSigners and connect means use getsigners and contract.connect(signer) to reproduce interactions from different accounts and validate access control and transfers.. In practical terms, test role-based behavior and cross-user interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Many test failures stem from a small number of recurring pitfalls. First, missing await on transaction calls can leave promises unresolved and cause assertions to read stale state. Always await the transaction and any required confirmations before checking state. Second, tests that share mutated state produce interdependent failures; deploy fresh instances in beforeEach to avoid that. Third, failing to assert revert messages means a test might pass even when the wrong revert reason or side effects occur. Use to. be. revertedWith to lock the expected failure reason. Fourth, not testing multiple signers or edge cases like zero-values and overflows leaves potential attack paths untested. For example, failing to test a require branch such as decrement at zero would miss a critical error path. Finally, assuming 100% coverage equals security is a misconception — coverage helps find untested lines but does not guarantee correctness of logic or resilience against complex attack vectors. Address these pitfalls by writing small, focused tests for edge cases, using clear revert assertions, and simulating competitor or attacker behaviors where appropriate. Running npx hardhat test compiles contracts and runs test files, producing console output that tells you which cases passed or failed and stack traces for failures. When a test fails, Hardhat prints the failing assertion and a trace showing the line in your test; inspect the test's preceding actions to understand the state at failure. For revert failures, the revert message appears in the assertion output when you use to. be. revertedWith, which helps confirm the exact reason for the revert. Use console. log sparingly inside tests to inspect values during debugging, but remove or comment them out when finalizing tests to keep output clean. Pay attention to beforeEach deploy logs; if a deploy fails, subsequent assertions will cascade failures. The terminal output is your primary debugger: read each failure carefully, reproduce locally by running the single test file, and iterate until the assertion and state align. As you practice, adopt a pattern of writing a failing test first for a new behavior, then implement or fix the contract until the test passes. Which failing trace do you usually inspect first — the revert reason or the state snapshot?

The assessment ideas in this chapter test your ability to select the correct Waffle matcher for a situation. For access control, when a non-owner tries to call an owner-only pause function, you should assert that the call reverts with the owner error, using to. be. revertedWith with the specific message. For balance checks after a deposit, use to. changeEtherBalance to measure exactly how an account's Ether balance changes after the transaction. These matchers express intent clearly and account for gas costs when appropriate. Practically, an assessment item might present you with a failing test and ask you to choose the assertion that confirms the contract enforces only-owner restrictions or that a deposit decreased the sender's balance by the deposited amount. When answering, prefer matchers that both confirm the economic effect and the revert reason; together they demonstrate that access control and funds movement are correct. Remember that the expect wrapper may accept a function that triggers a transaction when using change matchers. Keep four key ideas in mind as you write tests: First, tests are essential because smart contracts are frequently immutable after deployment, so catching bugs early is cheaper and safer. Second, Hardhat provides a local, deterministic network and injects ethers for contract deployment and signer simulation; always use beforeEach to maintain isolation. Third, Waffle matchers extend Chai with Ethereum-aware assertions such as to. equal, to. be. revertedWith, and changeEtherBalance; choose matchers that clearly express intent. Fourth, test both state and events and simulate multiple signers to cover role-based logic. Together these practices form a practical testing workflow: write focused tests, assert explicit revert reasons, validate emitted events, and simulate realistic user roles. These habits make your contracts more auditable and reduce the likelihood of surprising behavior after deployment. Which one of these practices will you adopt first to improve your test suite?

Keep these final practical reminders: write small, focused it cases; always await transactions and deployment calls; assert explicit revert messages to confirm error paths; and simulate multiple signers with contract. connect to test roles. In addition, test emitted events alongside state changes because events are part of the contract's observable A P I. Use Hardhat's deterministic network to run tests rapidly during development and view failure traces in the terminal to debug. Finally, treat test coverage as a tool, not a guarantee — aim for meaningful tests that reflect real usage and threat scenarios. Adopt these habits and your smart contract work will be far more resilient to regressions and unanticipated interactions. Which of these practical checks will you add to your next PR?
